title: Equation (7): one tree's contribution, as a failure profile

what.formal: Equation (7) composes the two mappings into a per-tree encoding: $\varphi_r^i(x, T_i) = \big(\mu_p(o_1)\mu_c(x,o_1),\; \dots,\; \mu_p(o_{|O_{\mathrm{in}}|})\mu_c(x,o_{|O_{\mathrm{in}}|})\big)^{\mathsf T}$ over the inner nodes $O_{\mathrm{in}} \subset T_i$. Its output dimension equals the number of inner nodes in that tree.
what.plain: Multiply each question's importance weight by its 0/1 answer, and line the products up into a vector — one entry per question in that tree.

what.note: A product of two scalars per node. Because $\mu_c$ is 0 or 1, each entry is either exactly $0$ or exactly the node's weight $\mu_p(o)$ — there are no intermediate values.

gloss.md: the $i$-th tree of the pre-trained ensemble
its set of inner nodes — its questions
the node's depth weight from Equation (6): larger near the root
the 0/1 content bit from Equation (5): 0 when the rule covers $x$, 1 when it does not

what.md: **The product is a mask, and this is the cleanest way to see what the vector is.** Since $\mu_c$ is 0 or 1, the multiplication does one of two things to each weight: it keeps it, or it deletes it. So the per-tree vector's nonzero entries are **exactly the depth weights of the questions this vertex fails.** Another way to say the same thing: the vector is a *failure profile* — a list of which questions failed, each valued at the importance of the question.

**Three consequences follow immediately, and all three are checkable.** First, a vertex that satisfies every question in a tree gets an all-zero block — the all-zeros case from Equation (5), now visible at the level of one tree. Second, the norm of the block measures *how badly* the tree explains the vertex: $\lVert \varphi_r^i \rVert^2 = \sum_{\text{failed } o} \mu_p(o)^2$, so failing a root question costs far more than failing a deep one. Third, two vertices that fail *the same set* of questions receive *identical* vectors, however different their feature values are. The encoding keeps only the pattern of pass and fail, not the margin by which a threshold was passed.

**That third point is a real limit and worth stating plainly.** A vertex with $x_2 = 2.01$ and one with $x_2 = 200$ both satisfy $x_2 \ge 2$ and contribute the identical entry. All the information about how far past the threshold a value lies is discarded. This is inherent to a threshold-based rule encoding — the same property that makes the encoding interpretable and cheap also makes it coarse.

example.md: **Walk 1 — the profile for four vertices.** Take tree $T_1$ with questions $x_2 \ge 2$ (depth 0) and $x_1 \ge 1$ (depth 1), and weights $\alpha = \beta = 6$, inside the paper's searched range, so $\mu_p = (1.000,\; 0.857)$.

items.why: The norm orders the vertices by how poorly the tree explains them, and it does so with the depth weighting built in: R, which fails only the root, scores higher than Q, which fails only a deeper question.

items.md: Now find a vertex that would tie with R. Any vertex satisfying $x_2 \ge 2$ but failing $x_1 \ge 1$ gets the same vector $(1.000, 0.000)$.
items.why: This is the coarseness in action. A vertex with $x_2 = 3, x_1 = 0$ and one with $x_2 = 1000, x_1 = 0$ are indistinguishable to this block — and would remain indistinguishable no matter how many vertices the dataset contains.

items.md: Finally, check the structure of the values: every entry is either $0$ or one of the two weights.
items.why: With $\alpha = \beta = 6$ the weights for depths 0 through 4 run $1.000, 0.857, 0.750, 0.667, 0.600$, so a block has only five possible nonzero values. **The embedding is not continuous in the depth — it takes a handful of distinct magnitudes.** That is a strong limitation on how much a downstream linear layer can differentiate, and it follows from the formula rather than from any implementation choice.

example.md: **Notice what the walk reveals about the whole design.** The rule embedding's information per vertex is: which of $C_r$ questions failed. That is at most $C_r$ bits, and after the depth weighting it is a vector whose entries come from a small set of magnitudes. Whether that is enough to improve node classification is an empirical question — and it is the question the paper's ablation is meant to answer, by comparing a model with this encoding against one without.

quiz.q: What are the possible values of an entry of $\varphi_r^i$?

opts.md: Any real number, since the weights are real
opts.expl: The weights are real but each is multiplied by a 0/1 bit, so an entry can only be the weight or nothing. No entry takes a value between zero and its weight.

opts.md: Either 0 or the weight of that node
opts.expl: Correct. The product of a real weight with a 0/1 bit is either zero or the weight itself, so the vector is a masked copy of the weights. This is why the block's nonzero pattern is exactly the set of failed questions.
That would be the content bit alone, without the depth weighting. The weighting multiplies in, so the magnitudes are the depth weights, not ones.

quiz.q: With $\alpha = \beta = 6$, a vertex fails one question at depth 2 and one at depth 3, and satisfies all others. What is the squared norm of its block? Give three decimals.
quiz.hint: Square each failed question's weight, then add. Ignore the questions the vertex satisfies.
quiz.sol: $\mu_p(2) = 1/(2+1) = 0.3333$ and $\mu_p(3) = 1/(3+1) = 0.2500$. So the squared norm is $0.750^2 + 0.667^2 = 0.5625 + 0.4444 = 1.0069$, which rounds to 1.007. Note that satisfied questions contribute nothing — the mask has deleted them.

quiz.q: Two vertices have $x_2 = 2.01$ and $x_2 = 200$ respectively, and identical other features. What does the rule encoding say about them?

opts.md: It distinguishes them, since one value is much larger
opts.expl: The rule is a threshold test. Both values pass $x_2 \ge 2$, so both produce a 0 in that slot — the margin is not recorded anywhere.

opts.md: It cannot distinguish them on that feature, because a threshold test discards the margin
opts.expl: Correct, and this is inherent to any rule-based encoding, not a defect of this implementation. What the encoding records is *which* predicates hold, not *how strongly*. It is the same trade that makes the representation interpretable: a threshold is cheap and readable precisely because it throws the distance away.

opts.md: It distinguishes them only if the tree is deep enough
opts.expl: Depth adds more thresholds, which can separate values the coarse thresholds merge — but only if the tree happens to contain a threshold between 2.01 and 200. The encoding itself never records a margin; it records where a value falls among the thresholds that exist.

close: **Next:** Equation (8), which assembles the per-tree blocks into one row per vertex — and this is where the embedding's width, and its main practical cost, become explicit.
